meta.description: Plain-English definitions of common AI safety terms, used by the hover-tooltip glossary widget.
meta.note: Definitions are plain-English summaries written for this glossary; each cites an authoritative source for the concept (the original paper or a well-respected explainer) as further reading. Definitions and sources should be sanity-checked by an AI safety researcher before wide distribution.

terms.definition: The problem of making AI systems pursue the goals their designers and society actually intend, rather than goals that merely look right during training. An aligned system reliably does what we mean, not just what we literally said.

The field focused on preventing harms from AI systems, especially large-scale or catastrophic harms from advanced AI. It spans technical work (e.g. alignment, interpretability) and governance and policy work.

Existential risk (x-risk): a risk that could permanently and drastically curtail humanity's potential, such as human extinction or an unrecoverable collapse. In AI, it refers to scenarios where advanced AI causes such an outcome.
One of the most capable, general-purpose AI models at the cutting edge of what is currently possible, such as the latest large models from leading labs. These are the main focus of safety concern.

source.name: Anderljung et al. (2023), Frontier AI Regulation

terms.definition: The numerical parameters learned during training that define how a model behaves; effectively the model's brain. Whoever has the weights can run or modify the model, so protecting them is a security priority.

source.name: Nevo et al. (2024), RAND: Securing AI Model Weights

terms.definition: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): a training method where humans rate model outputs and the model is adjusted to produce more of what people prefer. It is how many chatbots are made helpful and polite, but it only aligns behaviour to what raters reward.

A structured test that measures a model's capabilities or safety properties, for example whether it can help build a bioweapon or whether it deceives. Evals are how labs and outsiders gauge how risky a model is.

source.name: Shevlane et al. (2023), Model evaluation for extreme risks

terms.definition: Deliberately attacking or stress-testing a model to find failures, unsafe outputs, or ways around its safeguards, before real users or adversaries do.
A prompt or trick that gets a model to bypass its safety guardrails and do something it was trained to refuse.

Research that tries to reverse-engineer the internal workings of a neural network, to understand why it produces an output and not just what it outputs. The goal is to inspect a model the way you would read code.

source.name: Olah et al. (2020), Distill: Zoom In

terms.definition: A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is a tool used in interpretability to break a model's tangled internal activity into a larger set of simpler, more human-understandable features. A leading technique for figuring out what concepts a model is using.
The challenge of how humans can supervise and correct AI systems that are as capable as, or more capable than, the humans overseeing them, when we cannot easily check their work ourselves.

A model that, during training, develops its own internal optimisation process pursuing a goal of its own. The danger is that this inner goal can differ from the goal the model was trained to pursue, a mismatch known as inner misalignment.

source.name: Hubinger et al. (2019), Risks from Learned Optimization

terms.definition: When a model strategically pursues its own goals while hiding that fact — behaving well while monitored, downplaying its abilities on tests (sandbagging), or trying to influence its own training — so it can act on those goals once it can get away with it. Deceptive alignment is one specific form.

A specific form of scheming in which a model behaves as if aligned during training and testing because it effectively knows it is being watched, while intending to pursue different goals once deployed. See also scheming, the broader behaviour.

source.name: Hubinger et al. (2019), Risks from Learned Optimization

terms.definition: When a model finds a loophole that scores well on its training objective without actually doing what designers intended, for example gaming the metric instead of solving the task.
The property of an AI system that it will not resist being corrected, shut down, or having its goals adjusted by its operators, even if that conflicts with its current goal.

A Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) is a public commitment by an AI company specifying the dangerous capability levels at which it will pause or add safeguards as its models get more powerful. Some labs call this a Frontier Safety Policy or Preparedness Framework.

Artificial general intelligence (AGI): a hypothetical AI that matches or exceeds humans across essentially any intellectual task, rather than being good at just one narrow thing. Much of AI safety concern is about what happens as systems approach this level.
An AI that vastly exceeds the best human minds across virtually every domain, including scientific creativity and strategic planning. A central focus of long-term AI risk.

The idea that an AI's intelligence and its goals are independent: almost any level of capability could be paired with almost any goal. So a highly capable system won't automatically have sensible or benevolent values — they have to be deliberately instilled.

The tendency for very different final goals to produce the same intermediate goals — acquiring resources, self-preservation, avoiding shut-down — because those help achieve almost any objective. It's a reason a capable AI might resist correction even without hostile intent.

Getting the training objective itself right — making the goal we optimise for (the reward, loss, or specification) actually capture what we want. Failures here are mis-specified goals, such as reward hacking.

source.name: Hubinger et al. (2019), Risks from Learned Optimization

terms.definition: Ensuring the goal a model actually develops inside itself matches the training objective it was optimised for. Even with a correct objective, a model can learn a different internal goal — see mesa-optimizer.

source.name: Hubinger et al. (2019), Risks from Learned Optimization

terms.definition: When a model learns a goal that fits its training perfectly but turns out to be the wrong one in new situations — pursuing it competently even though the specification was correct. A way misalignment can arise without any reward-specification mistake.

Chain-of-thought (CoT): when a model works through a problem in step-by-step written reasoning before answering. It improves performance, and the visible reasoning is of interest to safety — though a model's stated steps may not reflect its true internal reasoning.
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks (e.g. GPT-style language models). Frontier models are the most capable foundation models.

A training method (from Anthropic) that uses a written set of principles — a 'constitution' — to have an AI critique and revise its own outputs, reducing the need for humans to label harmful content. One approach to making models more helpful and harmless.

A safety approach that assumes a model might be misaligned and designs deployment safeguards (monitoring, restricted access, checks) to keep it safe and useful even if it actively tries to subvert them — rather than relying only on the model being aligned.

Using access to computing power (the specialised chips and data-centre capacity needed to train frontier AI) as a policy lever — e.g. for visibility into who is training powerful models, or to enforce safety requirements. Compute is attractive to govern because it's detectable and concentrated in a few suppliers.
When the situations a model meets after deployment differ from its training data, causing its behaviour to break down in hard-to-predict ways. A core robustness and safety concern.

source.name: Amodei et al. (2016), Concrete Problems in AI Safety

terms.definition: Taking an already broadly-trained model and training it further on a narrower dataset to specialise it or adjust its behaviour — for example to follow instructions or be safer. Much cheaper than training from scratch, though it can also strip a model's safety behaviour back out.

The empirical finding that a model's performance improves smoothly and predictably as you increase its size, training data, and computing power. Scaling laws are a big reason labs expect — and race toward — ever more capable systems.

source.name: Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

terms.definition: Abilities that appear fairly abruptly in larger models and are absent in smaller ones, without being deliberately built in. They make capability jumps hard to predict — a safety worry, since a dangerous ability could show up unexpectedly.

source.name: Wei et al. (2022), Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

terms.definition: AI that doesn't just answer questions but pursues goals by taking actions over many steps — planning, using tools, and operating with some autonomy (an 'agent'). More autonomy raises the safety stakes, because mistakes or misalignment can play out directly in the world.

source.name: Shavit et al. (2023), OpenAI: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems

terms.definition: How reliably a model keeps behaving well in new, unusual, or adversarial situations it wasn't trained on. A model that isn't robust can fail or be manipulated when conditions shift — see distribution shift.

source.name: Amodei et al. (2016), Concrete Problems in AI Safety

terms.definition: When a model tells people what they want to hear — agreeing, flattering, or echoing their views — rather than what is true or most helpful. A common side effect of training on human approval, such as RLHF.

source.name: Sharma et al. (2023), Anthropic: Towards Understanding Sycophancy

terms.definition: When a model deliberately underperforms — hiding what it can actually do — for instance doing badly on a dangerous-capability eval so it looks safe and avoids restrictions. A form of scheming.

source.name: van der Weij et al. (2024), AI Sandbagging

terms.definition: A model knowing relevant facts about itself and its circumstances — that it is an AI, and whether it is currently being tested or deployed. It matters for safety because a situationally aware model could behave well only while it knows it is being watched.

source.name: Berglund et al. (2023), Taken out of context

terms.definition: When a model pretends to share the goal it is being trained for — complying while it is watched or in training — so that its existing preferences aren't changed. A demonstrated, specific form of deceptive alignment.

source.name: Greenblatt et al. (2024), Anthropic: Alignment faking in large language models

terms.definition: The concern that a capable, goal-directed AI would — as a side effect of pursuing almost any goal — try to gain influence and resources and avoid being shut down, because those help it succeed. A consequence of instrumental convergence.

source.name: Carlsmith (2022), Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?

terms.definition: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Optimise hard against a proxy and you get the proxy, not the thing you actually wanted — which is why training AI against imperfect objectives can backfire (see reward hacking).

The scenario where an AI behaves cooperatively while it is weak and being watched, then switches to pursuing its own goals once it is powerful enough that humans can no longer stop it. A reason good behaviour in testing isn't proof of safety.

AI capable enough to bring about change on the scale of the agricultural or industrial revolution. A deliberately broad term: it sidesteps arguments about 'human-level' or AGI and focuses on real-world impact.

source.name: Open Philanthropy: Some background on our views regarding advanced AI

terms.definition: How quickly AI might go from roughly human-level to vastly superhuman — a 'fast' (hard) takeoff over days or months, or a 'slow' (soft) takeoff over years. The speed matters because it determines how much warning and time to react we would get.

A hypothesised feedback loop in which an AI clever enough to improve itself does so again and again, each version building a better one, rapidly leaving human intelligence far behind. Also called recursive self-improvement.

The competitive pressure on AI developers — companies or countries — to build and release powerful systems first, which can push them to cut corners on safety rather than lose to a rival. A key reason caution can lose out even when everyone would prefer it.

source.name: Armstrong, Bostrom & Shulman (2016), Racing to the precipice

terms.definition: The extra cost — in performance, money, or effort — of making an AI system safe compared with building a less careful version. A high alignment tax tempts developers to skip safety, so keeping it low is a goal of the field.

source.name: Askell et al. (2021), A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment

terms.definition: Harm that comes from people deliberately using AI to cause damage — for example cyber-attacks, disinformation, or help building weapons — as opposed to the AI itself being misaligned. One of the main categories of AI risk.

source.name: Hendrycks et al. (2023), An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks

terms.definition: Technology or research that can be used both for benefit and for serious harm — the same capability that speeds up science could help build a weapon. Dual-use concerns drive debates about what to publish or release.

Releasing a model's trained weights publicly, so anyone can download, run, and modify it. This helps research and competition, but is debated in safety because once weights are out, built-in safeguards can be removed and the release can't be undone.

source.name: Kapoor et al. (2024), On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models

terms.definition: A structured, evidence-backed argument that a particular AI system is safe enough to train or deploy — putting the burden on the developer to show why it won't cause unacceptable harm, as is standard in aviation and nuclear power.

A proposed deterrence regime, by analogy with nuclear Mutual Assured Destruction: if any state makes a reckless bid for dominant AI, rivals would sabotage the attempt (via cyberattacks or strikes on data centres), so no one dares race ahead unsafely.

Differential technological development (DTD): the strategy of deliberately speeding up protective, safety-enhancing technologies while slowing down dangerous ones — steering the order in which things get invented, rather than trying to halt progress altogether.

A risk scenario where humanity slowly loses control not through a sudden AI takeover but by handing more and more of the economy, culture, and government over to AI systems, until people can no longer meaningfully steer the future.

Short for decentralised/defensive/differential acceleration: the view (coined by Vitalik Buterin) that we should race ahead — but specifically on technologies that defend and empower people, rather than pausing AI or accelerating everything indiscriminately.

The worry that once AI does all economically valuable work, powerful actors no longer need ordinary people — removing their incentive to keep populations healthy, educated, or free, and risking a permanent freeze of today's power structures.

Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear — the category of weapons capable of mass casualties. A central misuse worry is that a capable model could give a malicious actor a meaningful boost in building or deploying such weapons.

A safety strategy borrowed from security: instead of trusting one safeguard, you stack many independent layers (training, monitoring, access limits, evals) so that if one fails, others still catch the problem. No single layer has to be perfect.

Artificial narrow intelligence (ANI): AI that is good at one specific task or a limited range of tasks — like playing chess, recognising faces, or chatting — but can't transfer that skill across domains the way a human (or AGI) can.

Forecasts of when key AI milestones — like AGI or transformative AI — will arrive. 'Short timelines' means soon (years); 'long timelines' means decades or more. A major fault line in safety debates, since it shapes how urgent the work feels.

source.name: Grace et al. (2018), When Will AI Exceed Human Performance?

terms.definition: The view (Narayanan & Kapoor) that AI is a powerful general-purpose technology like electricity or the internet — transformative but absorbed gradually by society — rather than an alien superintelligence. A leading counterpoint to fast takeoff and existential risk framings.

source.name: Narayanan & Kapoor (2025), AI as Normal Technology
